findings.title: Shared coercion and range checks keep each rule in one place
findings.description:
`as_integer`, `as_real` and `require_real` are the only numeric coercion path. They are reused by `ConfidenceRange`, `SignalEvent` and `ParameterDeclaration`. `check_confidence` is shared by `LabelSeries` and `SignalSequence`. `_coerce` in `declarations.py` is shared by declaration construction and `bind_parameters`. This follows the DRY and "define once" rules.

The edge cases I traced are handled:
- `bool`, NaN and infinity return `None`.
- Integers above int64 return `None`.
- An `Integral` too large for `float` is caught as `OverflowError` and returns `None`.
- `2.0**63` returns `None` for `as_integer`, because the range check runs after conversion.
- Names and ids use `fullmatch` on an exact `str`, so a trailing newline and `str` subclasses are rejected.

findings.title: Exception handling, typing and error contracts conform to the Python rules
findings.description:
The only `try/except` is in `as_real`. It catches the specific `OverflowError` and has a comment explaining why returning `None` is correct. There are no bare or blanket catches.

`InvalidParametersError` passes `issues` as its single argument to `super().__init__`. Copy and pickle therefore rebuild the error correctly, and the tests cover `copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy` and pickle. The `TYPE_CHECKING`-only import of `ParameterIssue` avoids a runtime cycle between `errors.py` and `declarations.py`.

The code uses `|` unions and built-in generics, and `StrEnum` for permanent string values. `LabelSeries[I: (BarIndex, PointIndex)]` uses PEP 695 syntax, which matches the Python 3.12 target. I checked `require_iterable_of` and `require_instance` in `validation.py`. Their behavior matches how `Declarations` and `SignalSequence` call them. This includes naming a bad position as `field[index]` and rejecting a non-iterable.

findings.title: Tests cover the new behavior and the design constraints
Runtime `assert` used only for type narrowing
findings.description: `_require_series` calls `require_instance(...)` and then `assert isinstance(series, Series)` to narrow the type for pyright. The assert is redundant at runtime and is stripped under `python -O`. This is harmless, because `require_instance` has already raised. A `cast` or a typed return from the require helper would avoid asserts in production code. No action is required.

findings.title: Coupling of `_output_tuple` to `OutputDeclaration.__value__`
findings.description: `_output_tuple` uses `isinstance(item, OutputDeclaration.__value__)`, which relies on the `type` alias exposing its union at runtime. This keeps the allowed forms defined in one place, which is good. It does depend on a less common feature, and `test_declarations_reject` covers it. A new output form added to the alias is picked up automatically. No change is needed.

structured_findings.summary: Shared coercion and range checks keep each rule in one place
Exception handling, typing and error contracts conform to the Python rules
Tests cover the new behavior and the design constraints
Runtime `assert` used only for type narrowing
